guides.title: Indo-European Languages: Steppes, Anatolia & the Hybrid Origin Debate
guides.description: How Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Celtic, Slavic, Iranian, Germanic, and Hittite branched across Eurasia—and what 2023 linguistics and archaeogenomics reveal.
guides.intro: Stretching from Icelandic sagas and Welsh poetry to Persian ghazals and Sanskrit grammar before 1500 CE, the Indo-European family shares unmistakable regular cognates for kinship, wheels, yokes, and counting. Explaining how it spread bridges Bronze Age Yamnaya horse pastoralists with older Fertile Crescent farmers.
guides.scope: Reviews classical historical linguistics, cuneiform Hittite tablets, ancient Steppe genomes, and Heggarty et al. (2023) hybrid phylogenetic dates.

map.scope: Across Atlantic Celtic/Germanic, Anatolian Hattusha, Aegean, Russian-Ukrainian steppe, Tarim Tocharian, and Gandharan–Gangetic South Asia.

points.label: Pontic–Caspian Steppe (Yamnaya Corridor)
points.description: Major steppe pastoralist expansion contributing Bronze Age ancestry across Europe and Central Asia.

points.label: Hattusha / Central Anatolia (Hittite)
points.description: Earliest attested Indo-European cuneiform archives revealing archaic laryngeal-era features.

points.label: Taxila & Gandhara (Indo-Aryan / Prakrit)
points.description: Kharosthi and Brahmi Sanskrit–Prakrit inscriptions anchoring eastern Indo-Iranian branches.

points.label: Novgorod & Baltic–Slavic Crossroads
points.description: Medieval birch-bark vernacular Slavic letters alongside Baltic archaic morphology.

paragraphs.text: For decades scholars debated whether Indo-European spread outward from early Anatolian farmers (~8000 BP) or Bronze Age Yamnaya steppe herders (~5000 BP). Dense ancient DNA sampling proved both demographic pulses occurred sequentially across western Eurasia.

Heggarty et al. (2023) in Science proposed a hybrid synthesis from densely sampled core vocabulary trees (~8,100 BP root south of the Caucasus with later secondary steppe amplification into Europe and Central-South Asia), sparking lively integration with Steppe chariot and Tocharian Tarim archaeology.

sections.heading: Written monuments from Mycenaean Linear B to Vedic hymns

paragraphs.text: Comparing Hittite cuneiform archives (c. 1650 BCE), Mycenaean Greek Linear B clay accounts (c. 1400 BCE), oral-transmitted Rigvedic Sanskrit, and Avestan hymns anchored the comparative method that established regular phonological laws across Eurasian branches.

sections.heading: Maritime Latin–Romance, Slavic, and Indo-Iranian branches

paragraphs.text: Along Eurasia’s eastern and western extremes, Latin diversified into Mediterranean Romance languages while Middle Iranian (Sogdian, Persian), Indo-Aryan Prakrits, and Tocharian manuscripts along the Taklamakan rim documented Indo-European vitality deep across Inner and South Asia.
